chapters.summary: Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry calls the hearing to order, introduces herself as chair of the Committee on Small Business, and describes how rising rents and complex leases are displacing small businesses across the city. She frames the hearing around four bills aimed at helping businesses stay and grow.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry opens hearing and outlines the small business crisis

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This hearing is called to order.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Shanel Thomas-Henry, Chair of the Committee on Small Business, and thank you for joining today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: While traveling across the city to speak with small business owners, the one thing that kept coming up in these conversations is how hard it is for them to stay in this city and grow.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: With the goal of supporting our small businesses and keeping them in our community, this hearing will focus on discussing four bills.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: These are Introduction 90 from Councilmember Brewer, Introduction 408 from Councilmember Riley,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Introduction 578 from Councilmember Gutierrez, and Introduction 874 from Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the council colleagues, representatives from the administration, and members of the public for being here, as well as members of the public participating remotely.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We are losing our small businesses fast.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Last year, more businesses closed in New York State than opened.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Those businesses closed because we have made it too difficult for them to remain open.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The rising cost of rent in the city displaces not only our residents, but our businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This is a travesty because small businesses are the foundation of our city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They make a

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: get distinct, and they give it character.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They help define the neighborhoods they serve and can even become important social centers where people gather and interact in public, like barbershops and coffee shops.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Staying in business is no easy feat when small businesses are forced to navigate complex and expensive commercial lease agreements while also trying to find enough funds to continue to keep their business in operation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In New York City, the Department of Small Business Services exists to help support these business owners.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They help business owners navigate and adhere to regulations and provide them with funding streams when needed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The bills that we are hearing today would further allow SBS to fulfill its mission by centralizing tools to address the real and unique challenges our entrepreneurs face.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry walks through each bill: Intro 90 (Brewer) on commercial lease transparency, Intro 408 (Riley) on social media influencer matching, Intro 578 (Gutierrez) on IBZ Boundary Commission reform, and Intro 874 (Maloney) on a legacy business registry and preservation fund. She thanks staff and recognizes colleagues present.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry summarizes the four bills on today's agenda

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Introduction 90 from Councilmember Brewer would require commercial landlords to disclose information regarding the building prior to collecting rent on the property.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It also sets up procedures for negotiating lease agreements between business owners and commercial landlords and creates a private right of action for business owners to sue their commercial landlords for noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer's bill would help ensure that our small businesses could negotiate with their commercial landlords freely and without fear of losing their business in the process.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Introduction 408 from Councilmember Riley would help promote small businesses by establishing

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: a program to pair small business owners with local social media influencers to help market their business.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This bill would help ensure that our businesses are getting the promotional investment that they need to continue to operate in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Introduction 578 from Councilmember Gutierrez would reform our Industrial Business Zone Boundary Commission.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Her bill reforms the commission to make it less controlled by city agencies and more responsive to the community.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The bill also makes it harder to remove or shrink IBZs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez's bill would help ensure that our manufacturing businesses can continue to thrive in this city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And finally, Introduction 874 from Councilmember Maloney would establish a legacy business program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This bill would allow longstanding small businesses with community ties in the neighborhood to apply for funding and other assistance to keep them open in operation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney's bill would help preserve vital community landmarks and ensure that they remain open.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The legislation that we will hear today will help make our city more competitive by keeping our small businesses right here where they are.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing testimony from the Department of Small Business Services and hearing their positions on these bills.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I similarly look forward to hearing from small businesses and advocates on today's legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to thank Tyler Walls and Rebecca Barillo from

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: central staff for their hard work in putting this hearing together, as well as my own staff, Franklin Richards, Sierra Smith, Derek Slaughter, and everyone working in the background to help make this hearing possible.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I would like to mention that I am joined by my colleagues, Councilmember Brewer, Councilmember Maloney, Councilmember Santosuoso,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, I will now turn it over to Councilmember Brewer to provide opening remarks.

chapters.summary: Gale Brewer describes her years of advocacy for mom-and-pop stores and the task force report that led to Intro 90. She outlines the bill's key provisions including written lease requirements, renewal protections, pre-lease disclosures, cure periods, contact information requirements, and SBS oversight with model lease templates.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer presents Intro 90, the Storefront Business Bill of Rights

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for including this bill, Intro 90, the Storefront Business Bill of Rights, on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been working on this issue since 1980.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to let you know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Building on years of advocating for mom and pop stores as Manhattan Borough President, that wasn't that long ago, but it was 10 or so years ago, I convened a task force made up of small business owners, commercial tenants, and landlords.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To identify recommendations and proposals that would prevent small business owners from being priced out of the city, just because this is such a difficult issue to come up with solutions and get stakeholders to be supportive.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Months of substantive policy discussion focused on city fines and fees.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Unaffordable rent, scaffolding, construction, long-term vacancies, financing, and transitioning online businesses to brick-and-mortar.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: storefronts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This storefront business bill of rights intro 90 emerged from the task forces report small business big impact that we put together.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This report seeks to establish important protections for small business owners and improve communication between building and business owners.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A consistent message emerged.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Many small businesses enter lease agreements without access to essential information.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Then they face sudden rent hikes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Ambiguous lease terms, and a lack of predictability in renewal negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This lack of transparency and communication contributes to instability in the commercial market and business closures in our neighborhoods, neither of which benefits business owners or property owners.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Intro 90 responds to those concerns by setting clear standards for commercial lease transparency and renewal, creating a more stable environment for small businesses to thrive and plan into the future.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These are the key provisions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One, a written lease requirement for any storefront tenancy longer than one year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Ensuring clear and documented terms for all parties.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I will say that in many cases it's a handshake.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A handshake may be fine until the rent goes up and then you have nothing to base it on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, lease renewal protections, including the required $100,000.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 120-day notice of non-renewal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many times I know this pizza store.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Couldn't even get in touch with the owner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Never talked to the owner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The owner wouldn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He got evicted without any communication whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I couldn't get in touch with the owner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Three, mandatory pre-lease disclosure, such as a certificate of occupancy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is there one?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A breakdown of occupancy-related costs, utilities, taxes, fees, and a 10-year history of known violations or construction activity.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A reasonable cure period for up to 60 days for tenants to address lease violations except in emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Five, a requirement for both landlords and tenants to maintain and update contact information throughout the lease term.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And six,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Oversight by the Department of Small Business Services, which will also provide model commercial lease templates translated into multiple languages,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: along with user-friendly tools to help businesses estimate costs and understand lease terms.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I appreciate the continued support and dialogue with A&HD, the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, the New York City Hospitality Alliance, Webney, and of course, SBS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We all need to institutionalize these best practices.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I thank committee staff, Tyler Wells, Rebecca Baria, and Amman Mahara.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: As well as Chair Thomas Henry and Shula Puder from my staff.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I really appreciate this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's no easy answer to keeping small businesses in business.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We were just touring in Astoria and Jackson Heights.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think the commissioner was there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I could see, unfortunately, what happened on the Upper West Side happening there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Incoming, with all due respect, chain stores.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And they don't stand a chance against the mom and pops.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So hopefully we can give them that chance.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Virginia Maloney explains that legacy businesses are part of the city's fabric but face rising rents and operating costs. She describes Intro 874 as creating a registry for businesses operating 20+ years and a preservation fund to help at-risk businesses stay open.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney presents Intro 874, the Legacy Business Bill

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to Councilmember Maloney for opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Thomas Henry, for holding today's hearing and also for coming to District 4 to talk about Intro 874 and visit legacy businesses in my community.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Legacy businesses are part of the fabric of this city across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They're the neighborhood markets, the bookstores, the other family-owned businesses that have been here for decades.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And they're a big part of what makes New York so special.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It's unique character and identity.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But rising rents, skyrocketing operation costs are making it harder for these businesses to survive.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And when a longtime neighborhood business closes, we lose a piece of what makes that neighborhood uniquely New York.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I'm very proud of the Legacy Business Bill that we're introducing and talking about today, which will create a registry of recognized businesses.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: businesses that have served communities for at least 20 years and also have a preservation fund to help those at risk of displacement stay open.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: At its core, this bill is about giving long-standing small businesses the support they need to stay in the communities that they helped to build.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Haris Khan introduces himself and describes SBS's mission and recent initiatives including the NYC Future Fund, the Office of Street Vendor Services, the Cannabis NYC Loan Fund, the Coney Island BID, $8.4 million in neighborhood development grants, and the Open for Small Business regulatory reform package.
chapters.title: SBS Chief of Staff Haris Khan outlines agency accomplishments under Commissioner Minaya

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Chair Thomas Henry, Councilmember Brewer, Councilmember Murano, Councilmember Maloney, Councilmember Santoso, Councilmember Hanif, and members of the Small Business Committee of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: My name is Haris Khan.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I serve as Chief of Staff at the City's Department for Small Business Services, or SBS for short.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS's mission is to unlock economic potential and create economic security for all New Yorkers by connecting New Yorkers to good jobs, creating stronger businesses, and building thriving neighborhoods across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Over the past six months, under Commissioner Minaya's leadership, SBS has moved aggressively to deliver a new era for small businesses by advancing efforts to cut red tape, expand support, and reach more New Yorkers across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS revamped the $80 million NYC Future Fund to reduce barriers in lending, established the first-ever Office of Street Vendor Services four months ahead of schedule, and expanded the Cannabis NYC Loan Fund

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: to all New York City licensees.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS also helped create the city's newest business improvement district in Coney Island and released a

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: a total of $8.4 million in grants, one of the largest single releases of neighborhood development grants in our agency's history,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: to fund public arts, street cleaning, lighting, wayfinding infrastructure, commercial district marketing campaigns, and other neighborhood improvements.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The administration has paired our expanded programming with a historic regulatory relief agenda, including Executive Order 11 in January to inventory all fines and fees, and Executive Order 18

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: in July, the Open for Small Business package of more than 50 reforms.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: None of this work would have been possible without the direct feedback of small business operators through surveys, our direct service work, and roundtables led by Deputy Mayor Julisu with bodega owners, restaurant operators, and child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Commissioner Mania also held community partner convenings with a cross-section of local borough chambers, industry associations, merchant organizations, and hosted the agency's first ever

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: borough-wide bid convenings in all of the five boroughs alongside partner agencies and the first ever mom-and-pop czar, Delia Awusi.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: To ensure our work and the administration's commitment to transform the culture of city government reaches small businesses, Commissioner and I also joined Chair Thomas Henry, Councilmember Sanchez, Councilmember Salam, Councilmember Avila's, all in one day.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we joined Councilmember Zhuang's team, along with more than 70 volunteers and local partners to promote the update.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: business owner bill of rights as part of the Open for Small Business initiative.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: This year we've already reached 15,000 New Yorkers and small businesses through our work and we will soon unveil a new mobile outreach unit that will reach even more neighborhoods, bring more direct services to the doorsteps of mom and pop store.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Storefront operators and street vendors.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're grateful for the partnership of New York City Council as a critical partner in all of this work.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: This work would not be possible without your tireless advocacy on behalf of our small business community.

chapters.summary: Khan states SBS supports the goals of Intro 90 on lease transparency, supports a legacy business registry under Intro 874 but wants to discuss fund operational challenges, has concerns with Intro 408's social media matching pilot, and defers on Intro 578's IBZ commission reforms pending the administration's broader economic growth agenda.
chapters.title: Khan presents SBS positions on all four bills

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the bills attached to today's hearing that address some of the challenges businesses face.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Intro 90 would establish protections for storefront tenants, including requirements for a written lease of occupancy of more than one year, disclosure of fees, an option to extend leases in certain cases for up to one year with a cap on rent increases,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: an online commercial lease sample to be provided on the SBS website.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS supports the goals of this legislation, helping small businesses negotiate more affordable and transparent leases.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We are happy to be in further conversations with the bill sponsor on this bill.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Intro 874 would establish a SBS legacy business registry that recognizes businesses with 20 or more years of operation.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And establishes a grant program for legacy businesses at risk of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We are supportive of a legacy business registry, which would highlight neighborhood staples that form the city's cultural fabric and our local economy for years.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: On Brill provisions related to the Legacy Business Fund, we look forward to working with the sponsor to discuss ways we can mitigate possible operational challenges that may affect the success of such a program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Intro 408 would require SBS to create a matching pilot program for social media content creators and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We already offer digital marketing programming, including best practices for social media.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And although we support the intent of this bill, we have some concerns with the bill as written.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the bill sponsor on how we can expand this work to connect more small businesses with content creation and social media support, which is crucial to remain visible to prospective customers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Lastly, Intro 578 would amend the charter sections for the Industrial Business Zone Boundary Commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: While SBS provides educational programs and resources to meet all industrial business needs throughout the city through our programming, City Hall leads overall economic development policy, including the agenda for

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: including the development of a larger economic growth agenda that would include industrial and manufacturing businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So as Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Su are developing that citywide agenda for economic growth, we believe that should inform any further discussions and amendments related to the Industrial Business Zone Boundary Commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: With that, we appreciate the Council's attention to these bills attached to the hearing and welcome the opportunity to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There are also 16 proposed reforms in Mayor Mamdani's

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: open for small business package that requires the support of the City Council, and we look forward to working with all of you and your colleagues to usher in a new era for small businesses, one where city government is a partner.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The City Council's leadership in passing year-round outdoor dining, repealing the security grill visibility requirements, and other related reforms

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: paved the way for such continued momentum on these issues.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you again for this opportunity to testify and welcome any and all questions you may have.

chapters.summary: Frank Morano cites that only 13 Staten Island businesses were served by the commercial lease assistance program in FY2024 and asks how many applied, were turned away, or were even aware of the program. Khan explains no one is turned away, there is no backlog, and uptake correlates with the raw number of storefront businesses per borough.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions Khan on Staten Island commercial lease assistance uptake

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I would like to recognize that we have been joined by Councilmember Salam, and I do know we have a couple of hearings.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So in that, I will let Councilmember Marano ask his questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Kahn, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And thank you both for making an effort to visit the small businesses in my district.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It is great to have both a chair of this committee and a SBS commissioner and his chief of staff that

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: actually takes the time to visit and listen to small businesses themselves rather than think that's what reflected on reports and statistics is actually what small businesses are saying.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And obviously, I'm going to ask first about how this affects Staten Island small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to begin on the commercial lease assistance aspect of things.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to start with the number that jumped out at me in the committee report.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2024, the city's commercial lease assistance program

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Helped 685 businesses.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Of those, 252 were in Manhattan, 217 were in Brooklyn, and just 13 were on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's fewer than 2% of all the businesses served.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, I'm certainly not suggesting the city should distribute services based on borough population alone, but I want to know whether the need is being met.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many Staten Island businesses applied for assistance?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many were turned away?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And how many were actually made aware that this program exists?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you don't have those numbers, I'm wondering if you can provide them to the committee relatively soon, if not today, in the next day or two.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So on the commercial lease assistance program, no one is turned away if they want to start a new lease, renew a lease, or have landlord-tenant related disputes that do not rise to litigation.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so any business in Staten Island that reaches that, we would want to serve all of them.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We would want to meet all of them.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Nothing in our program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There is no backlog in the program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's no waiting list people get put on.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's some eligibility requirements to ensure they're not, and we can correct this if I'm wrong, but my understanding is they can't make over.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Couple million dollars every year in revenue, but if it's a small business, generally the ones that we visited together, all of them would be eligible to benefit from that service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it's one of the key programs we promote to all of our outreach work.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: This year, we've already reached 15,000 business

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: throughout the city, it's thousands of businesses in Staten Island as well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it does relate somewhat to borough proportions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So Brooklyn and Manhattan have a tremendously high number of businesses, raw number of storefront businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That number decreases in other boroughs and that impacts uptake.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Certainly doesn't impact our commitment to visit every business door to door, promote the programs, and then see if they're open to accessing the service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It also reflects to the issue of

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They may not want to engage in that service if things are going well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so that's another thing to consider.

chapters.summary: Morano points out that under Intro 874 a landlord could receive up to $22,500 while a five-person business gets only $2,500, and asks what safeguards ensure landlords pass benefits to businesses. Khan says the registry should move first and the fund requires further discussion with sponsors.
chapters.title: Morano questions Khan on Intro 874 landlord vs. business funding disparity

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Intro 874.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm a lover of legacy businesses.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Nobody cheered louder than me when the Carnegie Deli reopened yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I am proud to co-sponsor Intro 874, which is one of the many great ideas that Councilmember Maloney has already brought to this council in a short time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate the effort to preserve businesses that have become part of our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're the ones that sponsor Little League teams.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're the one that people have fond recollections of neighborhoods about.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's never a chain restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's always, you know, Joe's Diner.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I do have a question about where the money actually goes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Under this legislation, a legacy business could receive $500 per full-time employee.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A five-person business could therefore qualify for $2,500.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Meanwhile, a landlord could receive $450 per square foot up to 5,000 square feet.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's potential.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Essentially $22,500.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In that example, the landlord could receive nine times what the business receives.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What safeguards would ensure that a landlord receiving taxpayer money actually passes some meaningful benefit along to those businesses?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is one of many things that we're factoring in as we analyze this bill, which is why we think a registry, for sure, is something we should all move on as soon as possible and something we're really excited to develop as a result in partnership with all of you.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we also appreciate that in the bill, there is a nomination process where it's trusted community leaders like yourselves and others that would nominate and provide a rationale for who should be on such a registry.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That we think.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Should be one of the first things the city government does alongside all of you.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then on the fund, it requires further discussions with both the sponsors and internally in the city.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about the identity of the mayoral appointee representing the industrial community on the IBZ Boundary Commission. Khan explains the commission was last convened in 2014, its purpose is boundary designation, and the administration is developing a broader economic growth agenda that should inform any commission changes.
chapters.title: Morano questions Khan on Staten Island IBZs and the Boundary Commission

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have two final questions, one on industrial business zones and one on the social media aspect of things.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Staten Island has three industrial business zones, North Shore, Rossville, and the West Shore.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: These are important areas for businesses that need industrial space, including the kinds of businesses that depend on freight transportation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The committee report identifies something rather remarkable.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We apparently don't even know the identity.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: of the mayoral appointee who's supposed to represent the industrial and manufacturing community on the Boundary Commission.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that individual is, and can you tell us whether that person actually operates a manufacturing or industrial business?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the Industrial Boundary Commission was last convened in 2014.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's convened for the purpose of designating, modifying, or amending or repealing the boundaries of these industrial business zones.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's the purpose of that commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It doesn't impact programming and services that occur at the agency, and prior administrations have chose not to convene said commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: This administration is currently in the process of developing a larger economic growth agenda, which would include a focus on industrial and manufacturing businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we think that, depending on the process there, it should inform if the city would want to then...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Amend or consider other commissions and other entities and how they should function and the powers of said commissions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But in prior administrations, they've not convened this commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And probably they may have determined that the boundaries as existed sufficed for their purposes.

chapters.summary: Morano distinguishes between viral videos and real revenue impact, asking how SBS would determine whether the social media pilot generates actual customers. Khan agrees further discussion is needed and emphasizes SBS wants a scalable, curated program rather than one serving only a handful of businesses.
chapters.title: Morano questions Khan on measuring success of Intro 408 social media pilot

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Lastly, and thank you, Chair, for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm also a co-sponsor of Intro 408.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I recognize that social media can help small businesses reach a lot of new customers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I do want to distinguish between a successful marketing campaign.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and a viral video.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A restaurant could get a million views on TikTok and still struggle to pay its rent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How would SBS determine whether this pilot actually generates additional customers and revenue rather than simply producing impressive-looking social media statistics?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We similarly on this bill, we do think there should be further discussions on what should be codified in law on the services and the resources that are provided.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And completely hear you on the points you're making.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We think we have a base programming that exists and is resourced.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If resourced, we would be able to expand that base programming.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we would want to make sure it's very curated and carefully designed so that it is scalable, can reach all people, but it isn't so niche and specific that we could only reach 10 businesses in the city because of the extensive level of support we would be giving one or two businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We'd rather have something that enables people to make the decisions that they will make in the marketplace on what is best for them as they relate to social media.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: One thing that's clear for us, though, is we have to do more in this space, which is why we're excited to work with the bill sponsors here on something that would be workable and beneficial to the small business community.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to mention that we've been joined online by Councilmember Brooks Powers.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether the commission is defunct and whether 2014 members would still serve. Khan explains the commission could be convened today as members are office holders except the mayoral appointee, and that prior administrations chose not to convene it.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on IBZ Boundary Commission membership status

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions before I turn it over to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Going back to the industrial business zone boundary.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So is it essentially defunct or the members who were on there in 2014 are still technically members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So my understanding is quorum could be established today.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's not defunct in the sense that the membership of that commission, which includes elected representatives like the borough presidents and senior administration leaders like commissioners at HBD, finance, DCAS, SBS.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: President of the Economic Development Corporation.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Our understanding is that commission could be convened if there was a decision or desire by an administration to modify the boundaries of the industrial business zones.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We know in prior administrations, conversations have taken place on what zones should look like, but they have over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: In a couple years, prior administrations did not choose to pursue any amendments to those boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So if and when an administration, the city government, decides to modify the boundaries, then the commission could be convened.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, so the members are based on, I guess, appointments from various city agencies, not particular people at this point?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The charter states that the commission, this boundary commission is comprised of SBS, DCP, DOB, DOF, HPD, DCAS, EDC,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: and one member of the industrial manufacturing, associated with industrial manufacturing activities.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Alongside who would be appointed at the pleasure of the mayor, alongside

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: the five borough presidents.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So all of them are office holders, except the one appointee of the mayor.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Even without that one appointee, a commission could be convened if a decision was made to advance changes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So since it hasn't convened since 2014, everyone, no one from 2014 would be

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: in attendance at said meeting?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: With term limits, most likely yes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks what services the commercial lease assistance program provides. Khan describes pre-litigation services including lease review, up to 40 hours of pro bono legal support, and notes the program has served 3,700 unique businesses with 11,000 services since launch, including 1,850 in FY26.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on SBS commercial lease assistance program services

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Going to intro 90.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So with SBS current commercial lease assistance program, if I'm a small business and I come to inquire about this program, what type of services are provided?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The services we provide are pre-litigation services from starting a lease, renewing a lease, to landlord-tenant disputes that don't rise to litigation.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we're proud that this service has served thousands of businesses already across the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Since the launch of the program, we've provided 11,000 services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is over 3,700 unique businesses across all of the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it includes things like lease review, support and understanding what lease termination could look like.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Understanding liabilities, understanding how you would go about lease renewals.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's up to 40 hours of pro bono legal support, which is more generally sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we're really, really proud of that program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And under Mayor Mamdani,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: His leadership, the mayor has invested additional dollars to support an expansion of this program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: In a couple months, we will share, or a couple weeks, depending on how contract negotiations and the details land, we'll be really, really excited to share with all

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: of you an expansion of this program that would deepen the quality and the impact that we already see and are really proud of.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are there any, the 3,700 unique businesses, 11,000, are those for this year or since?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What's our time for it?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Those are programs since program launch.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have numbers, full fiscal year numbers from FY26, which in that year we served 1,850 unique businesses in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And any preliminary findings for this year as of yet?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We don't have that, and it does require some data deduping because we have a sufficient number of unique.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the numbers here, when we say 1,800, it does not reflect that those are the only types of– that is the number of services because a lot of the businesses that once they learn about the service, they benefit from the service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If they're opening up a new business or working with another on a partnership, they will then often reach out to us.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That number is only reflecting of unique businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So in last fiscal year,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've served over, we've provided over 1,850 unique services.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about recurring needs from businesses served. Khan says lease review is the most common casework, notes challenges for businesses with limited English proficiency, and describes SBS sending mailers to businesses from open data to promote programs. He confirms services are available in multiple languages with multilingual staff.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on biggest needs from commercial tenants and multilingual outreach

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What are some of the biggest needs from these businesses that you service that you're finding?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like what's coming up repeatedly for commercial tenants?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The vast majority of the casework is generally limited to or generally pertains to lease review.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So businesses often...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it speaks to Councilmember Brewer's bill where businesses may have trouble understanding that document and all of the implications of that document.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then if you add on other challenges like...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Other challenges that business owners may have, not having a lawyer in their partnership team that is opening up the business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It can be complicated if you're a speaker of English with limited proficiency.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's another complication now you have while you're navigating whether or not to sign that lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we know that the commercial rental market is not the easiest with plentiful options in every single corridor.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so businesses may be forced to make a decision in the interest of time to move without legal advice.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that's where we want to step in.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We want to serve those businesses ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: One thing we're really interested in doing and speaks to Councilmember Murano's point of

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Is there a backlog or why is it so few businesses that are partaking in the service?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We would love to do more.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we've even been sending mailers to businesses from open data with the state whenever we've seen data that suggests that a business may be opening.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Whether it's a residential address or a storefront address, we will send you a mailer that says we want to help you open.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Here's the program for business permitting, which is our NYC Business Express Service Team.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And here's the commercial lease assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If you haven't signed a lease yet, let us know and we want to help you understand what those terms are.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So really excited to keep working on this issue and also why we think we support the goals of Councilmember Brewer's bill of

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: some transparency and assistance to businesses in understanding what their liabilities would be in a commercial lease.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Those mailers, and then are they sent in multiple languages?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I can get back to you on the mailers and the languages, but all of our services are available in all the languages in the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Our team that provides this legal service is also comprises of multilingual staff.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the direct service of the legal advice can be provided in multiple languages as well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's not just relying on a third-party interpretation service.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS tracks lease renewal rates citywide. Khan says SBS only has data from businesses in their program, not citywide renewal rates, but does track citywide occupancy and vacancy rates and uses neighborhood development grants to address hotspot areas.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on commercial lease renewal rate data and vacancy tracking

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Does SBS currently have any data around lease renewal rates for commercial tenants?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like currently, are you tracking what rates are for tenants across all five boroughs?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We don't get access to data from businesses on the status of their lease

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: unless they're working with us in our program, and then they work with us on renewing the lease or negotiating with the landlord.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're very helpful sometimes helping businesses renegotiate some terms of their lease if they end up in a difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It was particularly common during COVID, and we're able to help save businesses thousands of dollars in back rent by renegotiating said leases.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the data we get on renewals is limited to the data that businesses are willing to share and provide us during casework.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: of what the businesses in themselves are sharing?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are you seeing any trends in different neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like similar to if you're renting apartments, there's certain market rate apartments depending on the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are you seeing those same particular trends as it relates to businesses?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we have and we analyze the citywide directory of database of storefront occupancy and vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It doesn't get us to the level of detail that would potentially let us know the implications on lease renewals and whether businesses are not getting their lease renewals.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They're choosing not to renew because of the cost of the lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That data doesn't currently exist, and there is no public data or data that businesses voluntarily share that provides that clarity.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But we do have general citywide occupancy vacancy rates that's tracked citywide, and that's how we get a sense of what the market is looking like in those particular neighborhoods where we know there's hotspots of prolonged and persistent

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: vacancy, sometimes chronic vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we leverage the neighborhood development grants that we issue, the $8.4 million, to provide some mitigation and support to those neighborhoods when there's applications from those communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have other questions, but I will turn it over to Councilmember Brewer to ask.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about the storefront database and whether there are trends away from handshake leases. Khan explains the database tracks occupancy and vacancy but not lease-level detail, and acknowledges verbal leases still exist, noting some businesses may prefer month-to-month arrangements over triggering renegotiation.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions Khan on vacancy database and handshake leases

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These are hard issues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess my first question would be, you're doing a great deal of work, but from my experience walking around Manhattan anyway, and now recently in the Queens,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: wonderful tour that we had.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is like a tidal wave to be able to be supportive of the mom and pops because the chains are like biting at the bit to get in there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, that was a perfect example.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I've seen that before in what we saw in Jackson Heights.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, I guess, does XYZ, that database, doesn't include some of the questions that the chair was asking, right?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That database, I call it the blaze database.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Does he put it together?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what does XYZ state?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know I should know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And how would that be helpful, if at all, to some of our questions?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's helpful in understanding larger occupancy and vacancy trends, not

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: in the level of specificity and detail that you're seeking to pursue where you'd have a greater granular understanding of lease renewal rates and the leases and the status of the leases and which ones are terminated and which ones are not.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Those are...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: A contractual relationship between the landlord and the tenant, and there currently is no disclosure requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Well, also the tenants, the commercial tenants, understandably never want to tell you what they're paying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've tried that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've had trouble getting a lot of information that we'd love to use for advocacy purposes, but businesses oftentimes are hesitant.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Understandably.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They won't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They won't tell you if they've got two sets of books.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They do not tell you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But my question also is, so many businesses...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Legacy or not, have no lease.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's a handshake, particularly when you're in an immigrant community.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Everybody thinks, oh, we've got a long-term relationship here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Well, not when, you know, somebody else comes calling.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I guess my question is, are you seeing some trends to get away from the handshake and no lease, or do you think that's still a big issue in our city?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's hard to tell because of the lack of specificity and clarity in the data, but it's definitely true that there are leases that exist without anything but a verbal agreement.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's also something to consider that in some cases the request for a written lease may trigger a renegotiation of terms that may not land more favorably.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: For some people, they may be making a calculation that what they're getting and what they got 10 years ago and what now they're getting on a month-to-month basis is better than anything in the market if they attempted to do a written lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it's a complicated issue with many factors, but that I'm sure is one of the things that businesses consider before they pursue.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But whenever we're doing the outreach, we're letting them know.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If you are about to sign a new lease or if you're going to be renegotiating a lease and you already had a lease, it's important for the business owner to know what they're signing on to again.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And oftentimes businesses may not find particular provisions of that lease relevant to them until, God forbid, an unfortunate incident takes place.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then it may be very important for them to understand those liabilities, but maybe a little late.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So that's why we, whenever we're doing our storefront outreach, we...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We can't predict which storefront is on which type of a lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Are they on a written lease or verbal?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But they should know that there's up to 40 hours of pro bono legal assistance available to them throughout the city with no wait time, no backlog.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They should reach out to us and get access to that.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what SBS advises when a business faces a massive rent hike. Khan says SBS provides rights and obligations information but acknowledges the affordability crisis, pointing to the mayor's Open for Small Business reforms and EO18's analysis of non-regulatory cost drivers including rent.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions Khan on what SBS can do for businesses facing 300-500% rent increases

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, but what can you do?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, you've always been able, and it's enhanced, to support these businesses.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But when you get a 500% increase in rent, that's when it's hard for SBS to do anything.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, or 300%, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What do you do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because I guess what my bill is trying to do is to say, I mean, first of all, like I said, I know businesses that can't even get the owner on the line.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, with SBS's help or help, they might be able to, but we don't reach them all.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So, and then they're just told, you know, 300% increase or get out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what we're trying to do is, A, say you have to talk, communication, and then some of the other things that we talked about, knowing what's, you know, what's in the building and the issues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then the more controversial part you mentioned, which is if there's no ability to negotiate, at least give at a 10% increase,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: give another year or six months, whatever it is, lease, so that that business at least has time to figure out what else they're going to do, and maybe they can work something out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's the pressure of the chain stores, for lack of a better word, is so intense.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I guess my question is, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you advise when a business has a 300% or 500% increase in rent?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is there anything that...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: SBS can do?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I mean, we're certainly not weighing in on like the business decision that businesses have to make, but we're providing them with all of the rights and obligations and understanding of those things.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So then they can make the informed decision.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But to your point, we are in the middle of an incredible affordability crisis that impacts New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And the mayor has been so eloquent on that crisis, but has also been eloquent on ensuring that people don't miss the fact that small businesses are also impacted by this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that is precisely why in July they launched, the city launched, we announced a 50-plus reforms package of open for small business, which will address some of the fines and fees on the government side that government imposes on small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But in EO18, which was accompanying that announcement, is also an analysis by SBS of all the other cost drivers that are not city regulatory imposed, but are cost drivers that we know businesses are struggling with

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: across the city and explore solutions to that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And your bill is one such proposal that could help mitigate some of the challenges businesses are facing with the high cost of rent.

chapters.summary: Brewer calls the Manhattan commercial rent tax horrible and asks SBS to add it to their list of considerations. Khan says he is aware of the CRT and believes state enabling legislation sets it up, and will take the concern back to City Hall.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer raises commercial rent tax as additional burden on Manhattan businesses

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll stop because my time is up.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Commercial rent tax in Manhattan, I hate it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It goes from Murray to 96th Street.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No other borough has it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We'd like to get rid of it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes, you're for that?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I think you're referring to the state commercial rent tax.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, it's the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Commercial rent tax goes from Murray Street to 96th Street, east and west.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's an extra tax that's left over from previous days.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In Manhattan, we want to get rid of it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Gorodnik got rid of some of it when he was in the city council.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We want to get rid of it for the storefronts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you could add that to your list of things that you're considering.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is certainly aware of CRT.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: OMB hell.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Certainly aware of CRT.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But our understanding is that there's state-enabling legislation that sets up the CRT system.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But we hear you, and we'll take it back to City Hall and our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: CRT is horrible.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, CRT.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how SBS tracks longstanding businesses being closed or displaced and the scale of the problem. Khan says SBS tracks occupancy and vacancy rates but not length of ownership, and notes complications like businesses that change ownership but keep the same name, such as Nathan's Hot Dogs.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney questions Khan on tracking legacy business closures and displacement

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I now turn it over to Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I would plus one my colleague from Manhattan on the commercial rent tax being an undue burden on Manhattan-based businesses south of 96th Street.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to turn to the legacy business bill, intro 874.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How does SBS, we've kind of gotten into this a little bit, but how does SBS track longstanding businesses that are being closed or displaced?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you have a sense of the scale of this problem?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We know that businesses of all ages, when we say it, businesses of all ages are impacted by closures and the challenges of running a business that are so varied across the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We, through the database and the tracking work that we do of occupancy and vacancy rates, we have a sense of how neighborhoods are shifting.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: how business rates are shifting.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It doesn't go into the level of detail on the length of ownership.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It also wouldn't tell us if ownership has shifted, but the business is the same, which I think is another level of data that may be interesting as we explore what it means to be a legacy business in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: A lot of them seem to be multi-generational.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Businesses, to your point.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But there's also businesses in Council of North Santoso's district, Nathan's Hot Dog, that transferred ownership and it was initially a family-owned business and is no longer.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And one may think if they don't follow up on the ownership status that it is still a family-owned business, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's owned by a...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Larger corporations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it's difficult and there's no clear precise data for this, there's no databases for this, which is why we support the registry proposal that you've made in the legislation in Intro 874.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We think a way by which

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: trusted, credible community leaders are identifying legacy businesses that have made contributions to the community and the city could benefit from additional marketing and

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: featuring them on a registry or a map would be something of interest to us where businesses could be promoted and New Yorkers who are interested in supporting those legacy businesses know exactly where to go, which intersection to go, and how to get in contact and

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: get the products and services these businesses have offered for generations of New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks what tools would best help longstanding small businesses facing displacement. Khan discusses challenges including succession planning, describes the worker cooperative business transition option, and provides the owner-to-owner transition hotline number for businesses looking to sell to their workers.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney questions Khan on best tools to help legacy businesses at risk of displacement

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What do you believe are the best tools to add a

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: help these longstanding small businesses, particularly with the displacement risk that we see.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: On the risks of displacement, we were concerned about the closures of any small business in the city, whether it's a business that just started a year ago or has been in business for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Obviously, there's larger impacts on the community if a business has been around, has had stable workforce, has employed New Yorkers, and then after 20 years has had to shut down.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: These challenges are so varied for some businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's simply sometimes it's just a challenge of succession when business owners, I forget the name of this pizza shop on 86th Street in southern Brooklyn, but it's a business that was around.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Pizza Wagon.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: No, they've been around.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But there's another one in Bensonhurst that recently shut down.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It was in that movie that everybody knows.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Anyways, this is going to be so annoying to me, and I'm going to remember it three hours later.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But this business was around there, a staple of the community for three decades.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Everybody knows this pizza shop except me.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Everybody buys from that pizza shop.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then they shut down.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And when I spoke to the business owners there since I was around there and was trying to understand if there was anything we could do, any lease assistance we could do, and it was just the business owner wanting to move to Florida.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's nothing else you could do if the business owner wants to move to Florida.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But one thing we're really interested in exploring and connecting New Yorkers to, something that exists already, but we want to make sure it's Lenny's Pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Lenny's 76 feet.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: One thing we're interested in is connecting New Yorkers of that nature, New Yorkers who love their business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They're really proud of the business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They just can't find somebody in their family or somebody else to buy the business off of them to consider selling their business, transferring ownership to the workers of that business so that business and the workers can remain in the community and continue to serve New Yorkers for generations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: New Yorkers can do that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Those businesses can do that by accessing our worker cooperative business development institute and the services there.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: One of them is the owner-to-owner.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Owners business transition hotline and it's 646-363-6592 or owners to owners dot owner to owners dot NYC which gets people connected to that service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So if we when we're promoting the service when we're promoting our work and we hear that a business is at this juncture where they're selling the business and we know it's not something

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: that could be managed any other way, they just want to sell the business, then that's something that we've offered for business owners.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I do.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether SBS has data on social media marketing trends and current engagement with social media companies and influencers. Khan describes existing webinars, the May Small Business Month Expo panel on content creation, and says SBS has relationships with social media companies and content creators but no in-house trend data.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney questions Khan on social media marketing data and SBS engagement with influencers

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If I can keep going.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
