utterances.text: I did want to ask a few questions, thank you, Chair, about the social media program of Intro 408, which anecdotally I've heard has really helped a lot of these businesses that are transitioning through the decades.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In fact, Council Member Shanel-Thomas-Henry and I visited

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: the luncheonette, which is in my district, and described revitalization after they got more involved in social media marketing, and everyone should go and try their milkshakes, which are the last homemade milkshakes actually

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: made fresh right there.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I've heard this anecdotal evidence, but curious if you've seen those trends citywide and if SBS has any.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Data on social media marketing and how that's helped small businesses, and also if SBS has any current engagement either with

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: social media companies or with the influencers that are creating the content and how you're thinking about pairing small businesses with that tool to help keep folks.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, to all of those questions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have relationships with the social media companies.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We also have relationships with the content creators in the social media landscape.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we also already have existing programming that seeks to promote digital marketing and leveraging social media.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have webinars that we do.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have events that we do.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have a social media marketing webinar on September 30th that's coming up soon.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And as part of our Small Business Month Expo, which took place on May 29th in Manhattan, where we had over 2,000, Shirtama Senri was there, 2,000 plus small businesses from all over the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We did a big marketing campaign.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We did boots on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: single borough try to promote this one-stop shop event so you could get connected with hundreds of different services, resources, not just the ones the city offers, but the ones the state offers,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: CDFIs and other affordable lenders, and just anything you could think of that could support a small business, including the commercial lease assistance right in front of you with direct service hours.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If you then learned about it and wanted to then have a consultation with the lawyer, you could also do that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And at that event, we specifically did a panel on how important the new content creation social media economy is for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we featured influencers that have worked with small businesses before so that they could learn more on best practices so they could also be part of this economy.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the first part of the question was if you have specific data on the trends or how small businesses are leveraging social media marketing.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We don't have any in-house trends that we're tracking or maintaining, but we know for a fact it is a vital and critical avenue for businesses to remain visible to customers.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It's a new reality.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's a new reality.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And for some businesses, they may be able to survive, including some of the legacy businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They have such a following, and the service or the product they're offering is one that doesn't require reaching new customers or engaging with customers every week.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Maybe it's a service that is...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Like your regular barbershop in the neighborhood may not have the same need to be on social media as another type of business where they constantly

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They need the churn of new customers who may not be coming there frequently for like their monthly appointment, but they need to ensure that they're constantly visible and attracting the right customer, especially in neighborhoods that are changing where there's population shifts.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So yes, very important.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's why we've baked in the service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We want to always and continuously improve on that service and would be really excited at the opportunity of resource to expand the programming on social media.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS formally partners with social media influencers. Khan describes working with influencer Dandy in the Bronx for the commissioner's appointment announcement and Megan Daly for BID education, and notes the mayor himself partnered with the chair to promote NYC Business Express services.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on SBS partnerships with social media influencers

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a quick follow-up question to those questions before I turn it over to Councilmember Santosuoso.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Does SBS currently partner with any social media influencers in particular in any way?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we've...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've leveraged social media influencers, as have some council members and other public figures, in leveraging them as just another form of reaching New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we've worked with Dandy in the Bronx, who's an influencer in the Bronx, to announce Commissioner Minaya's appointment alongside the formal press announcement and the mayoral announcement.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we're thinking of social media influencers as just another way to reach more New Yorkers, maybe.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Not all New Yorkers, maybe many in this room watch New York One a lot, but not all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: My wife certainly does not watch New York One.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: New York one.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we just want to make sure whatever platform, media, format New Yorkers are consuming, if we can find a way to get in front of more New Yorkers, we want to do that so our services are not just limited to the ones that...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: always are accessing these services, but are expanded to all that could be watching it, learning about it on different platforms.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we've done that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've also promoted our business improvement districts network and all the work we do with bids through a partnership

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: with Megan Daly, who's also a social media influencer that educated New Yorkers that are on her platform on what the bid does, which many folks are aware it's a pretty niche and specialized function.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Most New Yorkers may not know that they have a local community organization trusted by

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: council members, city government, resourced by property assessments of that community, making decisions for that community on how to improve those commercial corridors.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So is it more ad hoc or is it a formal process within SBS?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like if you're having, like the big event you guys had in May, do you have a list of partners that you would reach out to and say, hey, can you post this on your...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We wish we had a big list.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We barely have a list.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've just been whenever we've been pitching aggressively, just like with news media, where press teams across city government, they try their best to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We try our best to get the word out through the press core.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then we've also now started to get the word out, especially since the start of this administration, to get the word out with social media.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Content creators because we know they're reaching audiences that may not be typically accessed through news, New York One or New York Post.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: You have one of the most popular influences at your disposal at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The mayor.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And he worked with, and we got him to, and he wanted to work with you in promoting the New York City Business Express service team.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that was a great partnership of both our agency, you and Mayor Mamdani, and getting a really critical service out to eight plus million New Yorkers that learned about that program just through one video on May 29th.

chapters.summary: Kayla Santosuosso asks about anticipated operational challenges if SBS were required to create a content matching system. Khan emphasizes the need for clear expectations, guardrails, and careful program design, and expresses willingness to work with the bill sponsor.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso questions Khan on operational challenges of Intro 408 content matching system

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'll now turn it over to Councilmember Santosuoso.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Kahn, for your testimony and for being with us and for coming to Bay Ridge with the commissioner to announce the grants for the bids, which was much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Sticking with...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Sticking with the social media bill 408 that's in front of us, can you speak a little bit to some of the operational challenges that you anticipate if SBS were required to create this content matching creation system?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yeah, so we just want to make sure in any program and service that we're deploying and offering at the agency that it's clear what the expectations would be of the people that are providing said service and the consumers of that service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we also want to make sure that even if it's an emerging area that is important, the guardrails are equally as important and should not be loosened in any way.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so just wanting to ensure and would love to work with Bill Sponsor and Council on crafting expansions to any social media offerings that we have at the agency in ways that allows us to make them as responsible as possible.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we know that would be in complete alignment with members of the council as well.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso describes the Alpine Theater in Bay Ridge, the oldest independently owned cinema in NYC, facing $400,000 annual property taxes and potential closure. Khan acknowledges the issue relates to property tax calculations based on square footage and says it falls under DOF and City Hall policy.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso raises Alpine Theater property tax burden as legacy business issue

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I, as a co-sponsor of Councilmember Maloney's bill, which I'm excited about in terms of legacy businesses, you have heard me say this before, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Conby, you know that one of my most prized legacy businesses in Bay Ridge is the Alpine Theater.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Which is the oldest working movie cinema independently owned in all of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And when we're discussing sort of, you know, what makes legacy businesses close, this is a legacy business that wants to stay open, but can't and is probably eventually facing closure because their property taxes

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: amount to $400,000 a year property taxes for just one cinema.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And despite my, you know, screaming for help with, you know, the resources with the city and with the resources of the state, because I truly believe there must be an error that a single.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Theater that's independently owned, that's not fancy, that just has 10 theaters, like couldn't possibly be asked to pay $400,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I cannot get any answers and assistance from any department or any agency.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so I'm just once again, putting it out into the ether that if you have any suggestions as to how to solve this particular legacy business issue.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm all ears.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: You, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Khan, and the rest of the world that I'm saying it to.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: No, but on Alpine Theater, remember the first conversation we had on this, and I remember we, as we understand it, it's an issue of the square footage, and the square footage leads to that calculation, which leads to the dollar number you've cited.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so it's less of a discretionary choice, but rather how the property tax system and the calculations are made and how that then impacts a business

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: in your district that may not have been or may have been the intent of the decisions that were made on property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yeah, totally.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I just think the dynamic that ends up, you know, when we're talking about displacement of small businesses that result because of development, there should be in our tax policy a recognition that if a legacy business wants to stay, you know,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: whatever they purchased that property for, which of course is much less than it's worth in the modern day, they should be able to preserve that and resist whatever development.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: would turn them into a chain or, you know, some other sort of standardized business by having that reflect in the tax policy, because it does have a public benefit in order for those legacy businesses to be able to stay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So that I will just get off my soapbox.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But that was what I wanted to talk about today.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We love Alpine Theater and my wife, all of her favorite movies she's seen in Alpine Theater.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether SBS supports businesses in going online, noting that 30% online sales can be a lifeline for some businesses. Khan confirms SBS provides resources to help businesses digitize, integrate sales platforms, and compete in the online economy.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks whether SBS helps businesses with online sales platforms

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer has a follow-up question real quick.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Very quickly, and we were talking about influencers, but to my businesses, their big support mechanism for staying in business is like a 30% online if they have the kind of product that they can do online.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Without that online support, is that something that you also help people with?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, you've got a clothing, small clothing mom and pop owns.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You can't do that for milkshakes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, is that something that is also supported, advocated for by SBS?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, to help more businesses go online, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We think it's critical that businesses are able to, if they choose to, depending on the product and service they offer, compete on the online economy.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we've got resources to help business digitize and understand how do you integrate the different shopping platforms or sales platforms into your website and all the resources related to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether Executive Order 11's review of small business costs includes property tax issues. Khan clarifies EO 11 focuses on city-imposed fines, fees, and violations, while property tax policy is handled by City Hall, DOF, and OMB, though some state-level reforms have been identified.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on EO 11 scope and whether it addresses property tax issues

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Before I turn it over to Councilmember Salam, I just wanted a couple of follow-up questions to Councilmember Santos-Soso's bill.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Executive Order 11 in looking at reducing just costs to small businesses in general, do they look at property tax issues as they're related to Santos-Soso's question where...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The property tax policy is a larger and it impacts residential, commercial, all sorts of tenants and all sorts of property owners.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that's when that City Hall, DOF and OMB.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: work on.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The EO 11 charge that Mayor and Deputy Mayor Su placed on SBS and a whole set of regulatory agencies was one focused on the summonses, the violations, the fines and fees that are within city powers that do not require,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: some of them may require state action.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And in our 50 plus reforms package, we've identified state reforms such as the one where you may be required to have a state barber permit and a city

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: barber permit and have a occupational license as a barber in New York City or the ice cream, frozen dessert ice cream permit that you need in addition to your food service establishment permit.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we've identified some of these areas of duplication or just concerning regulations that create challenges for businesses trying to comply.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's what the EO 11 and EO 18 exercise was focused on, and we're really excited to keep deepening that work.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Of that work, 16 of those reforms, though, could move with the city council.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we're really excited over the next coming months and year to enact as many of those as possible so we can keep the momentum that the council has led on as well with the year-round outdoor dining bill, the quarterly payments bill, the repeal of the security grill requirement.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS could implement the social media matching program with existing resources. Khan says an expansion would require additional resources but SBS already has recurring social media marketing webinars built into programming and would welcome deepening the work.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on resources needed for Intro 408 implementation

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A quick follow-up question to Intro 408 as it relates to SBS rolling out this program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Would you be able to do it with existing resources, or would you need additional resources to...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We'd love to work with the bill sponsor to better understand what the program would end up looking like.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If it's an expansion of the program, it would require resources, but we already are serving New Yorkers with some level of...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Best practices on social media, digital marketing.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We want to deepen that work.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're really excited by that work, and we're proud to find ways to feature it more and more.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's that webinar on social media marketing happening on September 30th that all New Yorkers can access and businesses can access.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's also one on September 24th.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it's a recurring series that we already have built into our programming.

utterances.text: But certainly could always be expanding on that programming to reach more New Yorkers and have even stronger services on top of what already exists that we're proud of.

chapters.summary: Yusef Salaam notes Manhattan has the highest vacancy rate and asks for a breakdown for Community District 10 and corridors like 125th Street. Khan provides a 13.9% vacancy rate for the district, notes upper Manhattan and downtown have higher rates, and says the Manhattan average is around 13%.
chapters.title: Council Member Salaam questions Khan on Manhattan storefront vacancy rates in Upper Manhattan

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.text: And thank you, Mr.

utterances.text: Khan, for being here and visiting, both of you visiting my...

utterances.text: My district as well.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.text: But Manhattan can hide very different realities.

utterances.text: Can SBS break down how many of those businesses

utterances.text: We're in Upper Manhattan, and specifically in Community District 10.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Gotcha.

chapters.summary: Salaam asks what SBS does to connect Harlem residents to jobs in nearby Port Morris and Hunts Point IBZs. Khan explains the IBZ Boundary Commission's purpose is separate from workforce services, and describes the 18 Workforce One centers including one on 125th Street that connects roughly 22,000 New Yorkers to jobs.
chapters.title: Council Member Salaam questions Khan on connecting Upper Manhattan residents to nearby IBZ jobs

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And dealing with...

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Access to industrial jobs.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: None of the City's 21 IBZs are in Manhattan, but the Port Morris and Hunts Point IBZs are just across from Harlem River, from my district.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And they are real sources of good jobs for Harlem residents.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: What is SBS doing to connect Upper Manhattan residents to employment in nearby IBZs and does

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: the commissioner consider workforce access for neighboring communities when it weighs boundary changes?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the boundary changes

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The Industrial Business Zone Boundary Commission serves a purpose of determining, amending, repealing the boundaries that are set.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: In the city council and by the city government for what is the IBZ that then triggers a Department of Finance industrial business zone business relocation tax credit.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's the primary purpose of the Boundary Commission.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is separate and apart from serving industrial businesses, serving industrial workers, connecting New Yorkers in Uptown and in Harlem and other parts of the city to industrial and manufacturing business jobs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: All of that work is happening through our 18 Workforce One centers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's one in Harlem on 125th Street.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's the workforce center for most of Manhattan North.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we work closely with any and all large and medium-sized and even small businesses that want recruitment support to work with us and connect local New Yorkers and communities.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we're proud of that service, the Workforce One centers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We connect roughly 22,000 New Yorkers to...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: To jobs across New York and that's roughly similar to the 20 plus thousand New Yorkers we serve on the business services end.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So workforce is deeply ingrained in the work of this agency, even if we're called the Department of Small Business Services.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Gotcha.

chapters.summary: Salaam raises concerns that Harlem's Black-owned and immigrant businesses faced redlining and disinvestment, making 20-year track records harder to document. Khan acknowledges the concern and says SBS wants to work with sponsors on defining legacy business criteria, suggesting a nomination system with trusted community leaders.
chapters.title: Council Member Salaam questions Khan on protecting Black-owned legacy businesses under Intro 874

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'm going to move to

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Harlem specific, you know, Harlem's legacy businesses carry the cultural history of black America.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Many of them faced redlining, lost access to credit, and survived disinvestment that make a 20-year track record harder to document.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: How will SBS define significant contribution to history?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Identity or character so that black owned and immigrant owned businesses aren't disadvantaged and how will SBS weigh a community board's recommendations against the landmarks preservation committees since the two

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: may value different things.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you council member.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So on

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: On introduction 874, we would love to work with the bill sponsor to have further conversations and the city council on what would be a program that we could operationalize.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We do have some concerns.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We'd love to mitigate those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The points that you're making relate to some of those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's other concerns as well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But the point that we feel strongly about and in alignment with Councilmember Maloney 100% is we should be promoting legacy businesses, period.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And then it's a question of what would legacy business mean?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And the point we just made of there are businesses in the city and like in popular culture and in our psyche, we may think this is definitely a legacy business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But we may find out four years ago they sold interests to another private equity firm.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And now it's it's.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: and it's branded as family-owned, whatever, whatever, but it might not really be a legacy.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So what is a legacy business, I guess, is the more foundational question, which is why one way of going around it would be a nomination system of credible partners in the community, such as yourselves and the council,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: other leaders, such as the community boards, business improvement districts potentially, but all areas of potential collaboration where we're really interested in figuring out a way to deepen and expand the promotion of legacy businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about SBS outreach to businesses along Second Avenue affected by the next subway phase. Khan describes SBS services including financing assistance through CDFIs, and Thomas-Henry notes many Black and brown businesses prefer grants over loans and asks whether the administration has considered financial assistance for infrastructure-impacted businesses.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on SBS outreach to Second Avenue Subway-impacted businesses

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Salam.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: While we're in Harlem, I have a couple quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Second Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Has SPS visited, I mean, I'm sure there's a couple of legacy businesses or just any of the businesses in general that are along Second Avenue where the Second Avenue subway face.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Next phase is happening.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, we've been in that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Frankly, those businesses are in crisis at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So are there any resources that you have been able to provide to them to help them weather this storm?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we at SPS have the services that you're very, very familiar with at this point, Chair Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So those are the services that we have.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And one service that could be helpful to a business that is seeking some bridge funding to continue operations would be financing assistance.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we don't connect small businesses in the city to the larger banks.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We connect them to CDFIs, community depository financial institutions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: institutions that provide affordable lending options to small businesses on more affordable terms.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we've done outreach in Second Avenue, we've done outreach throughout Harlem, and when we connect New Yorkers to financing assistance, we're looking at more affordable lending options as a tool for them to use to manage their operations.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Well, I will say this, especially because a lot of those are black and brown businesses, they don't traditionally like

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: lending and would prefer more of a grant or even some just assistance considering that this is a project that is out of their control.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Yes, it is needed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Other municipalities, when they're developing such large infrastructure projects, put parameters in place where there is financial assistance available to those that are significantly impacted.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is there anything that the administration has thought of to provide similar assistance?

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry presses on whether the administration has considered providing grants similar to other municipalities during major infrastructure projects. Khan notes the Second Avenue project is an MTA project, says such a program doesn't currently exist in the city, and mentions Council Member Salaam's related bill on construction grants is under review.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on MTA responsibility for Second Avenue Subway business assistance

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the Second Avenue project in particular is an MTA project that the MTA is carrying out.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So theoretically, if entities that were managing major capital projects, millions if not billions of dollars, if they allocated funding for such a purpose and wanted to work with SBS, we would work with them.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But that type of a program, as you mentioned, may have existed in other jurisdictions but doesn't exist in the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We're looking for a nudge from the admin to help convince them to provide.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We understand there's a council bill that Councilman Yusef-Salaam has introduced.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: that would also seek to provide grants for roadway construction.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we know the administration is reviewing it and we're in active conversations on ways to tailor the program.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS has ever referred businesses to the state's historic business registry. Khan says SBS's legacy-specific service is the worker cooperative transition option, and notes 6,400 businesses with 20+ years of operation have benefited from SBS programs overall.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on referrals to state historic business registry and legacy business services

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In terms of legacy businesses, has SBS ever referred businesses to the state's historic business registry?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So currently our legacy business services are just the same services we provide every single business with the exception that if a business owner, I'm sorry, even in that exception, it applies to every business.

utterances.text: If a business owner is selling their business and don't have a succession plan in place, we connect them to that opportunity of.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is the primary legacy business service.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan

utterances.text: businesses that have benefited from our program that were in operation for 20 or more years.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: To our work.

chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on investigating high vacancy areas and landlord behavior

Khan says businesses don't typically ask about purchasing and SBS doesn't have a specific service for it, but notes SBS does connect businesses to SBA loans for property purchases when requested.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on whether SBS advises businesses on purchasing vs. leasing property

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I would say in some of the, well, I'm going to just speak for the outer boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And even on some of our tours in some other districts, I've heard from tenants who are currently about to go through lease negotiations, mentioned that when they first went into the premises, that they were offered the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Opportunity to purchase the property under the

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: commercial lease assistance program or any programs within SBS, do you guys do any type of counseling as it pertains to

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: speaking with small businesses to show them the options as if they were to take this lease or to just go ahead and purchase that property, what that could look like and do for their business?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Seeing that a lot of the pitfalls from these.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The businesses that reach out to us are asking for support with the lease assistance piece of the issue that they're navigating when they're starting a business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They don't reach out to us on purchasing, but we also don't have a service for purchasing, so that may explain.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It can be an option because a business, as a former business owner, sometimes you don't know what options are available to you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Almost similar to renters who think they can't be homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Sometimes all it takes is someone asking the question, have you considered this?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And is that something where SBS could do just a simple projection?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because if you're leasing...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A space at X amount per month for an X number of years, what's the benefit versus buying that space and not having to worry about that lease renewal 10 years from now?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A whole lot in that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I mean, it's interesting in that when we did the walkthrough in Harlem with Councilmember Salam and we asked the business owner, my understanding of that conversation was they would never even dare to dream of buying that building because of the rate, the market rate price of that commercial property.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we're in a situation where businesses are struggling to hold on to their commercial leases.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it's tough to envision a scenario where it would be a very popular service to offer to businesses to buy in this current market condition, maybe in a condition where there's some level of availability.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Of commercial storefront stock that allows for more options.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It would help not only on the tenancy side, but it would also help with the purchasing.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I did want to make a correction.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: When businesses, when they do reach out to us saying they need money, significant amounts of money, our whole financing operation does support with that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we even...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Connect New Yorkers to some of the SBA loans that are available for the purchase of properties.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So there is the resources that already exist.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We are connecting New Yorkers to those, but when they ask for that resource.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I think your question was more, would we go out and ask a business owner if they're interested in purchasing property?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just advising, like when they come in to speak about their current lease, just if it's something they thought of.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks what advertising resources are available to small businesses. Khan describes digital marketing support, social media best practices, and the Link Local program with LinkNYC kiosks that provides neighborhood-based advertising with an easy-to-use template for business owners.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on advertising resources available to small businesses through the city

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Going back to introduction 408, currently, what are the different advertising available to small businesses through the city?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So on 408, we provide digital marketing supports.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We provide social media support and understanding how and what the best practices are to engage with these platforms.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We also work with Link Local, which is with Link NYC on a program we've jointly supported called Link Local, where we provide neighborhood-based advertising for small businesses and community organizations

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: on Link NYC kiosks across the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So that's another way by which businesses can engage in access-free and digital marketing.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that service, there's an easy-to-use template for business owners.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They don't have to go through a complete, very, very complicated process to get their business up on these Link NYC kiosks and another partnership and collaboration with Link NYC to get that done.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS cross-promotes its various services when a business comes in for one program. Khan confirms SBS cross-promotes all relevant services during outreach and direct interactions, noting they serve 22,000 businesses annually and many become repeat clients.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on cross-marketing of SBS services to businesses

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And is all that made available to businesses when they come to SBS in general?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like, say I come for the commercial lease program where the representatives say, hey, when you open up, use this resource.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This is available to you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So do you cross market the various resources that SBS offers from beginning to end, no matter what the client comes in for?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we cross-promote the services no matter what the

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: small business owner came in for when they speak to our outreach team or when they speak to our NYC Business Express service team or the small business advocates that are in our agency and generally make it a practice as soon as a business owner shares.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: they could benefit from or they are challenged with another issue that relates to another service, we've got the resources.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've got dozens and dozens of free resources.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's just a matter of establishing that relationship.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We also are protective of that relationship.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We know even when we do door-to-door outreach on something as simple as the business owner bill of rights, which the mayor has, through EO18, required

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: city agencies to start distributing at the beginning of inspections starting October 1st, even in sharing this flyer of the business owner bill of rights, as many of you are familiar with door knocking

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: in residential buildings, it's also similar in commercial corridors where businesses may only have the attention.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Of five seconds, if not less, in some of these interactions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we want to protect them by ensuring that we're directing the most relevant message to them in that moment.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But when the opening makes itself available, where they're expressing interest in potential other services or just sharing needs that they have in the city that they could benefit from,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: our SBS services, we would cross-promote in that moment 100%.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's the practice and helps us serve the 22,000 businesses we serve every year.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And a lot of the services we provide end up being a good substantial amount of them are repeat New Yorkers, repeat small businesses that once they learn about the service, they want to...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They want to use it more and promote it with the friends and family members who are also in small business community.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how to ensure demographic equity in legacy business nominations and assistance, noting Queens has many legacy Black and brown entrepreneurs. Khan says SBS wants to work closely with the bill sponsor and committee on all parameters including equity criteria.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions Khan on ensuring equity for Black and brown legacy business nominations

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have one final.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Question before I turn it back over to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So Queens, similar to Harlem, does have a lot of legacy black and brown entrepreneurs and that could potentially qualify for the bill.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are there any recommendations on how we can ensure equality and demographics for nominations and eventual legacy appointments and assistance?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: At this time, we'd love to work closely with the bill sponsor and the committee to have further discussions on all the different parameters we should consider.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That would be one.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's so many other criteria that the city and city council should consider if this bill advances in the legislative process.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks about partnerships with LinkNYC, Made in NYC, and private companies like Neon for a social media pilot. Khan confirms the LinkNYC partnership, describes workforce development collaboration with Made in NYC (MoM), and says he'd like to learn more about Neon and other private matchmaking platforms.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney questions Khan on LinkNYC, Made in NYC, and private matchmaking companies for social media pilot

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I wanted to ask a bit about some of the resources that are available citywide to help with a pilot program for the social media outreach that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So my question is, do you partner with LinkNYC to help promote small businesses and promote them?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And another group to mention would be Made in NYC.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And private companies that kind of serve as this matchmaker like Neon.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm just curious how you'd think about all these different players in a pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So, yes, we do work with LinkNYC very closely, and it's a longstanding partnership at this point now.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we also then organize for them webinars and other educational ways to reach more New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So they operate the program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's their LinkNYC kiosks.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're building the pipeline, so more New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: workers and small businesses can benefit from them in addition to their own outreach work that they are conducting.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I forget the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Made in NYC.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Oh, so made in the MoM.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Which has helped small businesses before with marketing, if that's something you've plugged into as well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we work with MoM really closely.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's more so on the workforce development side as when...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've got joint partnerships where we're training New Yorkers interested in post-production careers, other job training programs like production assistant.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's one of the closest and most deepest areas of our partnership, but our leadership teams are always in conversation whenever we could benefit from collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We always do so, and Commissioner Espinal and Commissioner Minaya every other week almost are either speaking to each other or seeing each other.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the last category is private companies that are serving as this matchmaker now, like Neon.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I would love to learn more and we can discuss further.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We do work with EDC as well.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So when EDC has programs where they're convening small businesses or startups or they have the founders fellowship, for example, there is other cross training, cross promotion opportunities where they're aware of our programs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We are aware of their programs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so there are opportunities for all of us to work together.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Definitely we'll learn more about the program that you're referencing in particular.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry opens the floor for public testimony, reminds attendees of decorum rules, no recording from the witness table, two-minute time limits, and instructions for submitting written testimony within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry opens public testimony and announces procedures

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's topic.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come up to the table once your name has been called.

chapters.summary: Whitney Hu reads a statement from Adam Glenn, owner of Jimmy's Corner, urging the Council to support the Small Business Rent Stabilization Act (Resolution 496), which was pulled from today's hearing. She emphasizes that rent is the core driver of business closures and all four bills are good but insufficient without rent stabilization.
chapters.title: Whitney Hu testifies on behalf of Small Business United urging commercial rent stabilization

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now I will call.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The first panel, Whitney Hu, Ki Sang Yi,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Francesca Bruce.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Francesca Bruce.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I'm here.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Amoris Grulin.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Whitney, you begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: You're going to kick me off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: My name is Whitney Hu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: I'm here on the behalf of the Action Lab, which is working with a coalition of small business owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: I'm actually going to read a quick statement from our founding steering committee member, Adam Glenn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: He is the owner of Jimmy's Corner, which is one of the longest running bars in Times Square, is black owned, and it is actually in a process of possibly losing their space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: He wrote, while we appreciate the New York City Council and Committee on Small Business working to support small businesses, if we want neighborhood businesses to survive in New York City, we have to deal with what's driving so many of us out, the rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: We were disappointed that Resolution 496 was pulled from today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Small Business United, SBU, had organized business owners from across our coalition to come testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Because this issue matters that much to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: The Small Business Rent Stabilization Act is the kind of systemic solution small businesses have been asking for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Small business owners need stability and predictability so we can plan for the future, grow our businesses, invest in our workers and communities, and not have everything we've built threatened by unpredictable and unsustainable rent increases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Commercial rent stabilization is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: isn't just about keeping today's businesses open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: It's about making sure the next generation of small business owners can afford to open their doors in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Without that stability, we're not just losing businesses, we're making it harder for new ones to get started.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: Small business owners are telling the council what we need to survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: We need our leaders to listen and take on the issues that will determine whether we're still here 5, 10, or 20 years from now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: For too many of us, the question is whether we'll even make it through the next year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: And I would just add Small Business United.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: I think all the bills presented today were wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: And Councilmember Brewer would love to talk to you about your bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Whitney Hu
utterances.text: But I think for us, Resolution 496 and the fight that's about to happen on the state level is really important to us.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Francesca Bruce of the Grand Street BID in East Williamsburg supports all four bills, highlighting that nearly half of storefronts are minority or women-owned and 35% report declining business. She describes Intro 874 as reforming perverse displacement incentives, Intro 90 as leveling the playing field, and Intro 408 as going beyond education to direct assistance.
chapters.title: Francesca Bruce testifies in support of all four bills on behalf of Grand Street BID

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and thank you all so much for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: I'm Francesca Bruce with the Grand Street Business Improvement District in East Williamsburg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: You might remember me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Supporting all the bills championed here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: The sweat equity of our small businesses, particularly our immigrant and MWBEs, has made our beloved neighborhood what it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Today, nearly half of our storefronts are minority or women-owned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: The vast majority rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Amidst exploding rents, vacancy rates higher than the citywide average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: 35% of our merchants reported declining business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Yet these merchants have zero control over the forces that determine whether they survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: And these intelligent and timely bills speak exactly to our needs and recommendations, as my colleague here will elucidate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: In 874, the Legacy Business Registry and Preservation Fund offers real survival tools to legacy businesses, including direct grants to legacy businesses and long-term incentives for landlords to lock them in and keep them in the face of speculation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: While this may seem expensive or landlord-oriented, it in fact accomplishes a very rare feat of reforming and balancing a perverse incentive structure that favors displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: 22% of our businesses have been here 20 years or longer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: These are critical legacy institutions, and they are at high and immediate risk of displacement, so we support this bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: In 90, the storefront business bill of rights levels a drastically unequal playing field, helping to slow the engines of speculation, commercial warehousing, gentrification, and displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: And 408, the content creator matching program, goes beyond the typical SBS approach of mere education to ensure smaller businesses who may not have time for an expo or funds to implement SBS recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: can actually afford and secure direct assistance on a critical tool to adapt, grow, and remain economically viable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Together, these bills stabilize our community, honor our history, and give small businesses a genuine chance to endure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: We urge you to pass all of these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Bruce
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ki-Sung of the Grand Street and Graham Avenue BIDs describes East Williamsburg's legacy businesses, with 22% operating 20+ years and the oldest in continuous operation for 97 years. He notes businesses lack administrative capacity for certifications and succession planning, and urges systemic, proactive support beyond conventional loans and webinars.
chapters.title: Ki-Sung testifies on legacy business needs in East Williamsburg

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: My name is Ki-Sung, and I currently serve the neighborhood of East Williamsburg in my capacity as the Commercial Revitalization Program Manager at the Grand Street bid and the Graham Avenue bid as a port of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: By SBS's Avenue NYC program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: As my colleague Francesca Bruce has testified, we are here in support of all these bills attached to today's hearing, and I'd like to provide further testimony that points to the critical need to implement Bill 874.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: As evidenced in our forthcoming Commercial District Needs Assessment Report, our neighborhood has a strong representation of legacy businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: 22% of them have been at their current location for over 20 years and are oldest in continuous operation for 97 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: They lend to the neighborhood's celebrated character as having old-school family vibes and local mom-and-pop shops where multi-generational families can continue to age in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: For instance, Metropolitan Fish Market supports an entire commercial ecosystem by supplying to households as well as local restaurants and delis, while St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Herman Music Shop has been sponsoring the neighborhood's Three Kings Parade and Hispanic holidays for generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: These businesses are embedded in the neighborhood's identity and they have local street cred, but what they do not have control over is their long-term tenureship in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: The beloved Crest Hardware has closed and local bookshops like Quimby's and Desert Island have been displaced due to high-rise luxury developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Similarly, the economic development observed in North Brooklyn in general, as measured by metrics such as aggregate sales tax records, hides the gentrification and displacement experienced by East Williamsburg's legacy commercial and industrial businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Our businesses who operate with an average of two full-time employees lack the administrative

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: strut of our

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: financial capacities to pursue the certifications, regulations, financing mechanisms, and even the basic succession planning that can help sustain their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: So respectfully, conventional loan options and webinars do not reach the family-run operations in our neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Instead, there's a patent need for systemic, proactive, and equitable support to ensure that these strongholds can remain in the neighborhoods that they serve with additional

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: coordination, hopefully, with DOB, DEP, DSNY, and other agencies to more effectively operationalize the bill spirit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ki-Sung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Amauris Gurujung, co-founder and CEO of Bronx Native, describes how social media and content creation helped grow his business and strongly supports Intro 408. He argues connecting local businesses with content creators benefits both businesses and local creative talent.
chapters.title: Amauris Gurujung testifies in support of Intro 408 social media matching program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Thomas Henry and members of the New York City Council Committee on Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: My name is Amauris Gurujung.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: I'm a Bronx-born creative, social entrepreneur, content creator, co-founder and CEO of Bronx Native.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: I started Bronx Native in 2015 with a mission to change the narrative of the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: What started as a clothing brand has grown into a cultural platform, retail space, creative hub, and community that uses storytelling to uplift our borough and the people and businesses in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: A huge part of that growth has come through social media and content creation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Platforms like TikTok have allowed us to tell our own story, reach thousands of people beyond our neighborhood, bring customers into our businesses, and create opportunities that we simply would not have had access to other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: but also see firsthand that many amazing small businesses across the Bronx and New York City don't have the time, resources, or know how to effectively tell their stories online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: That is why I strongly support Councilmember Kevin Riley's Intro 408.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Connecting local businesses with content creators can be extremely powerful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Creators understand how to tell stories, reach audiences, and turn online visibility into real-world attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: For a small mom-and-pop shop business, that can mean new customers, increased foot traffic, greater sales, and ultimately keeping their doors open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: And this benefits creators too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: It creates paid opportunities for local talent to use their skills while investing directly back into their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: I've seen the power of content firsthand, not only through Growing Bronx Native, but also by using our platform to highlight other local businesses and organizations across our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: New York City has incredible entrepreneurs and incredible creators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Intro 408 gives us an opportunity to connect the two and strengthen our neighborhoods in the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: I respectfully urge the council to support Intro 408.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amauris Gurujung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: I would like to focus my remarks on Intro 90.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: I support, like most of the commercial brokerage community, reasonable transparency and protections for small businesses in the leasing process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: But Intro 90's mandatory one-year lease extension could introduce significant uncertainty into a market that serves tenants and landlords alike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: First, this proposed legislation is being introduced at a time when New York City's retail market is thriving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Small businesses are opening and expanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Available space has declined along many prime retail corridors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: And tenants'rents generally remain below pre-pandemic levels in many parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Second, owners already have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: have strong incentives to reach agreements that retain successful and reliable tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Replacing a tenant means marketing the space, paying brokers, negotiating a new lease, and accepting the risk that the storefront may remain vacant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: I've seen time and time again that an owner will work with a proven tenant who has been there for years rather than start over with an unknown business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Third, commercial spaces are often committed to new tenants months before an existing lease expires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Under this legislation, an existing tenant can unilaterally remain for another year, potentially leaving a new business that has already spent money, hired employees, or planned an opening around a specific date without access to the space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: It's not fair and it's not great public policy, especially since

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Major global companies could take an extension the same way a small mom and pop could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Lastly, this would affect more than property owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Newer, smaller businesses often lack the financial history or operating experience of established tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: This uncertainty...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Of a mandatory extension would introduce, that the mandatory extension would introduce could make owners cautious to lease to them, only making it harder for entrepreneurs to open their doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: The council is right to support small businesses in transparency in the leasing process, but this can be accomplished without disrupting negotiated leases or creating uncertainty for the small businesses waiting to occupy these spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Steve Soutendijk
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and consideration.

utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Retail broker Joanne Podell, a former small business owner, argues the retail market is strong and successful tenants renew early. She contends the mandatory extension would delay the next generation of businesses and make owners less willing to take chances on new entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne
utterances.text: However, I have concerns that some provisions of Intro 90 will do the opposite, as Steve has mentioned.
